answer.read: Ravensteiner is capacity-full and allocates seals (Z capacity_full, news:20260822-23). It wants binding volume and long terms (Z planning_security) and holds 56 d lead as a stability point. It moved only half a euro on our 36-month, full-volume sheet (offer:70410-1) and accepted the should-cost data while defending its margin. Its status is open, not final, so there is room to push. Rubber and labour indices give it a catch-up argument. The part is single-sourced, so the relationship charge matters: we must not squeeze it below a sustainable margin.
answer.message: Thank you for acknowledging the full volume and the long term, which gives you the binding planning security you asked for. In return we need a firm commitment that matches our production rhythm, so our sheet keeps the three-year commitment and asks for our required lead time instead of the extended one. Our purchase history on this part also shows where a fair level sits for a committed long-term customer. We are confident this gives both sides a stable basis.
answer.reason: o4 keeps the three-year full-volume commitment the supplier values most and moves lead time to our required forty-two days. On the code's prices that cuts our C to about the same level as o3, o5 and o6, below E0, o1 and o7. Its supplier-side value matches E0. o4 has the lower health price of the 42-day options, so we stay further from the relationship-charge zone than with the 35-day mixes. A 35-day lead would strain a capacity-full supplier for no extra C benefit. A 24-month term would undercut the planning security that is its strongest need. E0 accepts the 56-day lead and costs us more. The order-history citation anchors the price with a new kind of argument. The supplier has already heard the index data, which favours it, so we leave that out.
